content: During the meeting, any conflicts of interest that were deemed insignificant enough to not compromise the guideline development process or its credibility were managed by requiring experts to openly declare such conflicts at the beginning of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting. No further actions were taken in these cases. Annex 3 provides a summary of the declarations of interest (DOI) and outlines how the WHO Steering Group addressed conflicts of interest declared by invited experts. Decision-making during the GDG meeting The GDG reviewed and discussed the evidence summary during the meeting, seeking clarifications where necessary. In addition to assessing the balance between the desirable and undesirable effects of the intervention and the overall certainty of the evidence, the GDG applied additional criteria from the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework to determine the direction and strength of the recommendation. These criteria included stakeholder values, resource implications, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. The considerations were informed by the experiences and opinions of GDG members and supported by evidence from literature searches where available. EtD tables were used to describe and synthesize these considerations. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the participants. None of the GDG members opposed the recommendation. Document preparation Before the online meeting, the WHO Steering Group prepared draft versions of the GRADE evidence profiles, evidence summaries, and other relevant documents for the GDG’s deliberations. These drafts were shared with meeting participants two weeks prior to the meeting for their comments. During the meeting, the documents were revised based on participants’ deliberations and remarks. After the meeting, the WHO Steering Group drafted a full guideline document to accurately reflect the discussions and decisions of the participants. This draft was electronically sent to the GDG and the External Review Group (ERG) for final review and approval. Peer review Following the GDG’s review and approval, the final document was sent to eight external independent experts (the ERG), who were not involved in the guideline panel, for peer review. The WHO Steering Group evaluated the feedback from the peer reviewers for inclusion in the document. Post-meeting and external peer review, the WHO Steering Group made only factual corrections and language improvements to enhance clarity. Recommendation and supporting evidence The recommendation and its supporting evidence are outlined in the subsequent sections. The EtD framework, summarizing the balance between desirable and undesirable effects, the certainty of the evidence, stakeholder values and preferences, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, and equity, is presented in Annex 4. The GDG adopted the following recommendation: Umbilical vein injection (UVI) of oxytocin is recommended for the treatment of retained placenta only in the context of rigorous research (research-context recommendation). Evidence from trials comparing UVI of oxytocin versus expectant management and UVI of oxytocin versus UVI of saline suggests that this intervention may reduce the need for manual removal of the placenta. However, its effects on other priority outcomes, such as infections, maternal satisfaction, and length of hospitalization, remain unclear. While cost-effectiveness is unknown, the additional costs of supplies required for this intervention are likely negligible. No other UVI regimen was shown to be superior to UVI of oxytocin when compared with other solutions or uterotonics. Remarks The GDG acknowledged the potential of UVI of oxytocin in treating retained placenta but found the evidence of benefit in reducing manual removal of the placenta insufficient to recommend its routine use in clinical practice. The group emphasized the need for high-quality randomized trials comparing UVI of uterotonics with expectant management in women with retained placenta to assess its impact on severe postpartum hemorrhage-related morbidity and mortality, in addition to reducing manual removal of the placenta. In research contexts, the use of this intervention should be considered only in cases of retained placenta without abnormal bleeding. UVI of oxytocin is likely effective only in treating placenta adherens, the most common type of retained placenta, which results from failed contraction of the retroplacental myometrium. To date, studies have not distinguished subtypes of retained placenta prior to treatment, which may have contributed to the lack of efficacy observed in some cases. Dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of the recommendation The dissemination and implementation of this recommendation should involve all stakeholders in maternal health care at international, national, and local levels. Efforts should focus on increasing women’s access to maternal health care and strengthening the capacity of health-care facilities to provide high-quality services. The recommendation should be integrated into care packages and programs at country and facility levels, where appropriate. Dissemination will occur through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. The recommendation will also be available on the WHO website and the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during scientific conferences and meetings attended by WHO maternal and perinatal health staff. The document will be translated into six United Nations languages and disseminated through WHO regional offices. Technical assistance will be provided to regional offices for further translation if needed. Adaptation National and subnational subgroups may adapt and implement this recommendation based on existing strategies. This process may involve developing or revising national guidelines or protocols based on the updated recommendation. Global models, such as those for WHO antenatal and intrapartum care guidelines, can be adapted to different countries, contexts, and the individual needs and preferences of women. These models aim to improve the quality of maternal health care by achieving optimal physical, emotional, and psychological outcomes for women and their babies, irrespective of generic policies within and across health systems and countries. The successful introduction of evidence-based policies depends on well-planned, participatory, consensus-driven processes of adaptation and implementation. Implementation research considerations UVI of oxytocin is recommended only in the context of rigorous research due to important uncertainties about its effectiveness. Implementation can proceed on a large scale if conducted as research addressing unanswered questions about effectiveness, acceptability, and feasibility. Stakeholders, particularly those involved in postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) prevention and treatment programs, should be informed of the current lack of sufficient evidence to recommend for or against UVI of oxytocin for retained placenta. Providers and women should be made aware of these uncertainties. This recommendation should not detract from the importance of high-quality postpartum care, including the use of uterotonics, tranexamic acid, intravenous fluids, and blood products. Rigorous research, ideally through randomized trials, is needed to assess effectiveness. There is no standardized dilution regimen for oxytocin in UVI, with doses ranging from 10 to 100 international units (IU) and saline volumes from 10 to 30 mL. Injection methods include direct injection into the umbilical vein or via an infant mucus aspiration catheter introduced along the vein to 5 cm from the placental insertion. The use of a catheter with an additional 30 mL of saline has proven more effective in reaching the placental bed than direct injection. Research implications The GDG identified critical knowledge gaps requiring primary research, including: 1. Is UVI of oxytocin more effective than expectant management in reducing PPH-related maternal mortality and morbidity? 2. Is UVI of oxytocin more effective than intramuscular or intravenous oxytocin administration in reducing PPH-related maternal mortality and morbidity? 3. Is UVI of other uterotonics (e.g., carbetocin, prostaglandins) more effective than UVI of oxytocin in reducing PPH-related maternal mortality and morbidity? 4. Is UVI effective only in certain types of retained placenta, and can these types be accurately diagnosed clinically before UVI? Anticipated impact on care organization and resources If UVI of oxytocin is proven effective, updated training curricula and training for relevant health workers will be required. Measures to ensure a sustainable supply of oxytocin and necessary injection equipment, typically available in maternity care settings, will also be needed. Monitoring and evaluating guideline implementation As this recommendation is research-context specific, its implementation should ideally occur within high-quality randomized controlled trials to address uncertainties about its benefits and harms. If implemented in routine care, its impact on health outcomes should be monitored at health service, district, and national levels. Broader efforts to monitor and evaluate maternal and newborn health care quality should not be neglected. Monitoring activities should adopt clearly defined review criteria and indicators aligned with WHO standards for improving maternal and newborn care quality. Updating the recommendation The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) convenes annually to review WHO’s maternal and perinatal health recommendations and prioritize new and existing questions for development and updating. This recommendation will be reviewed and prioritized accordingly. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendation may be updated. If no new information is identified, the recommendation may be revalidated. Following publication and dissemination, any concerns about the recommendation’s validity should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for updates. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in updated recommendations.
